title: On the large deviations behaviour of acyclic networks of G/G/1 queues
contribution: Gives a large-deviations calculus for single-class acyclic networks of G/G/1 queues: Assumptions B and C on arrivals and service survive passing through a queue, superposition and Bernoulli splitting, so waiting-time and queue-length tails at every node, with their most likely paths, follow by induction (the 1994 LIDS report version of S177).
problem_entry: {SD; AP (packet networks) as motivation} Loss probabilities of order 1e-9 call for tail estimates (p. 3); network results were only bounds of unclear tightness (p. 3); the closest prior G/D/1 departure result (dVCW93) rests on a technical assumption not re-verified for the departure process, so its inductive use is doubted (p. 4).
key_idea: Impose LD Assumptions B and C on external arrivals and service, prove that each operation (queue, superposition, Bernoulli splitting) preserves them, and induct over the acyclic network, 'a calculus of acyclic networks' (pp. 8-10); self-contained without the Dembo-Zajic result (p. 4); most likely paths read off the optimizers (pp. 12, 22-23).
assumptions: DAG in which any two directed paths meet at most once (p. 7); single class, FCFS (p. 3); stationary possibly dependent interarrivals, iid service, Bernoulli routing, independence across nodes (pp. 3, 7); E[A] > E[B] (p. 11); Assumption B one-sided LDP for arrivals and Gartner-Ellis for service (pp. 9-10); Assumption C sample-path LDP lower bounds from Mogulskii or mixing (pp. 10, 43-45); iid service weakenable to a mixing condition (p. 24). No data.
proof_devices: Gartner-Ellis theorem with one-sided rate functions for tail probabilities (pp. 5-7)

waiting-time LDP taken from the literature ('This result is not new', proof omitted) with the most likely path as the optimizer of an infimum over empirical rates; matching bound omitted (Theorem 4.1, pp. 11-12)

distributional-law relation (queue length seen by a customer >= n iff customer 0 is still in the system) extended beyond renewal processes; lower bound by dualizing a constraint on theta (Lemma 4.2, Theorem 4.3, pp. 13-16)

departure LDP: sample-path upper bound (Prop. 5.1, pp. 17-18) and a lower bound on a forcing set where every customer finds the server busy (Prop. 5.2, Lemma 5.3, pp. 19-22), matched by conjugate calculus (p. 20)
departures' log-MGF returned as a convex dual so the induction continues (Theorem 5.5, Corollary 5.6, pp. 24-25)
special cases: G/D/1 reproduces dVCW93 'exactly', M/M/1 recovers Burke's theorem in the LD regime (pp. 26-27)
Palm and time-stationary laws share LD behaviour via Walrand's relation and Hoelder's inequality (Theorem 6.4, pp. 31-32); superposition (Theorem 6.1, p. 28)
Bernoulli splitting by Stirling counting (Theorem 7.1, pp. 36-37)
experiments: One Matlab example: two tandem queues with deterministic servers (rate 3.87) and two-state Markov-modulated deterministic arrivals (mean rate 3.29); theta1* = -18.62; departures smoother than arrivals; theta2* = -infinity, so no large queue at the second node. No simulation, no failures (pp. 39-41).
positioning: Extends dVCW93's inductive G/D/1 approach to continuous-time G/G/1 networks while doubting its inductive use; avoids Dembo-Zajic's technical result; reuses the group's own distributional laws (Bertsimas-Nakazato, Bertsimas-Mourtzinou) (pp. 3-4, 13).
writing: Hedged criticism of the closest work ('not very clear to us', p. 4); 'It is instructive to' remarks drawing most likely paths after theorems (pp. 11-12, 25, 38); a side result offered as 'of independent interest' (p. 4); omitted proofs announced (pp. 11-12).
limits_future: Single class, acyclic, paths meeting once (pp. 7, 41); two proofs omitted (pp. 11-12). Open problems: feedback, several traffic types, scheduling policies chosen in the LD regime (p. 41). Versions [card s04, S177]: the journal version's card records deterministic splitting, theta1* = -9.47 in the same example and the departure theorem as 5.4 (here Bernoulli splitting, -18.62, Theorem 5.5; pp. 24, 36-37, 40).

method_links.note: Optimization is the analytic language, not a solved model: rate functions are infima over empirical-rate paths whose optimizers are the most likely paths, constraints are dualized to match bounds, and convex duality returns the log-MGF for the induction; no solver class. Context: Tension T3.
Written with the co-adviser Tsitsiklis and their co-advised student Paschalidis (card s04), whose thesis on the subject is cited as in preparation.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: closure calculus for decomposition
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Departure, superposition and Bernoulli splitting preserve Assumptions B and C, so each queue is analysed alone by induction; existing name (card s04).

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: most likely path as an optimizer
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The most likely path to a large waiting time or a departure deviation is the optimizer of the rate-function problem, drawn for the single queue, the departures and the tandem example; existing name (card s04).

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: subsume the incumbent as a special case
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The G/D/1 case reproduces dVCW93's discrete-time result exactly, and the M/M/1 case recovers Burke's theorem in the LD regime.

transferable: For a network-wide tail result, define an input class by LD assumptions, prove each elementary operation (queue, merge, split) maps the class into itself, and induct over an acyclic graph, restricting the topology (paths meet once) so merged streams stay independent (pp. 7-10).
Get a matching lower bound from a forcing set of sample paths (every customer finds the server busy, so departures equal services) and match it to the upper bound by convex conjugacy (pp. 19-20).
Check a new calculus against the classics first: reproduce a published special case exactly and a textbook theorem (Burke) in the new regime (pp. 26-27).
When one stream is seen from another stream's arrival epochs, prove first that Palm and time-stationary laws share LD behaviour, then use the time-stationary one (pp. 28-32).
coauthors: Ioannis Ch. Paschalidis, John N. Tsitsiklis

quotes.text: However, we should note that it is not very clear to us how the large deviations result for the departure process in [dVCW93] can be applied inductively.
In this way, our approach provides a calculus of acyclic networks since we will be able to determine the large deviations behaviour of each individual queue inductively.

title: A critical survey of optimization models for tactical and strategic aspects of air traffic flow management
contribution: Reviews air traffic flow management optimization models by class (single- and multi-airport ground holding, deterministic and stochastic; the generalized tactical problem), naming in each the best available model, its computational record and applications, and concludes that strong formulations already solve realistic instances, with computation and manager acceptance as the obstacles to adoption.
problem_entry: {AP + IO; SD for the stochastic models} Congestion costs airlines 'well over $5 billion per year' (p. 2); flow management by ground holding and flow redistribution is the short-term remedy (pp. 2-3); task: best available models, contexts, formulations and solution methods from more than 40 references (p. 1), organized by a taxonomy of four classes (pp. 4-5).
key_idea: Review as triage: per class the best available model, its computational performance and applications, and a verdict (p. 1). Deterministic single-airport Model 1 is a transportation/assignment problem (pp. 9-11); stochastic static and dynamic Models 2-3 are 'the most advanced existing models' (pp. 7, 11-19); the authors rank their own Bertsimas-Stock model first for the tactical problem (pp. 23-24) and cite Andreatta-Brunetta's comparison for the multi-airport case (pp. 28-29).
assumptions: Single-airport network with one capacitated airport, deterministic travel times, known delay costs, T periods (p. 7), justified for the US (over 95% of delays at airports) but not Western Europe (p. 8); Model 2 with few scenarios (4 or less), 3-4 cost classes and a constant air-delay cost (pp. 12-13, 16); all network models deterministic, re-solved when conditions change (pp. 23, 27). Data cited: FAA OAG schedules, a EUROCONTROL set (p. 26), Boston Logan (p. 22).
proof_devices: Model 1 as a transportation problem convertible to an assignment problem, hence polynomial (p. 11)
total unimodularity of Model 2a so the LP suffices, solvable as min-cost flow (p. 14)
unimodularity of Model 2b left as Richetta-Odoni's conjecture from integral LP runs, 'still an open question' (p. 15)
integral LP relaxations of Bertsimas-Stock explained in part by connectivity constraints being facets of the convex hull (p. 27)
solve device: network-flow core without capacities for a basis, then capacities added and dual simplex (p. 27)
two-flight probability-tree example: static cost $1,000 vs dynamic $920; dynamic strategies favour long-range flights (pp. 19-22)
experiments: Bertsimas-Stock on FAA data: 278 flights/10 airports/178 sectors (43,226 constraints, 18,733 variables) integral LP optimum in about 30 min, 1,002 flights/18 airports/305 sectors in about 2 h (SUN SPARC20, CPLEX 3.0, GAMS 2.25) (p. 26); vs EUROCONTROL's CASA (Vranas 1995): about 40% less delay in 3 of 5 cases, about 5% in two, CASA in about 30 s, feasibility not clearly checked, 'very preliminary' (p. 26); multi-airport runs of 1,000 and 3,000 flights at the infeasibility border, CPLEX MIP 2.1, up to 9,411 CPU s, one instance 4% non-integral (pp. 29-30); Boston Logan tests of Models 2-3, no controller-in-the-loop test (p. 22).
positioning: Credits Andreatta-Romanin-Jacur with the first optimal ground-holding approaches and Terrab with the first multi-period models (p. 9); judges STN 'quite disappointing' and MAS opaque (pp. 24-25); ranks the authors' own Bertsimas-Stock model first, backed by Andreatta-Brunetta's comparison (pp. 23-24, 28-29).
writing: Report style with four numbered objectives and numbered conclusions (pp. 1, 30-32); a verdict per class; draft traces: Model B/D/E/F labels for Models 1-3, a mislabelled table caption, a wrong section reference (pp. 10-11, 14, 19, 29-30).
limits_future: Single-airport models assume uncapacitated en-route airspace (p. 31); stochastic single-airport work not extended to multi-airport problems (p. 27); computation and 'the difficulty of gaining TFM manager acceptance' as obstacles (p. 31); further research 'strongly encouraged' (p. 31); priority-rule heuristics may become an alternative (p. 29); a Part II on capacitated flow models announced (p. 8).

method_links.note: Models judged by formulation strength (total unimodularity, integral relaxations, facets) and solve time on realistic data; 'strongest formulations proposed to date' is the closing verdict. 1997 practice of the strong-formulation mark SKILL.md dates to the 2005 IO book (Tension T4).

The owner's operational rule (EUROCONTROL's CASA, first planned first served) is the baseline and the optimizer's own cost (30 min-2 h vs 30 s) is printed with the evidence called very preliminary; but the comparison is a third party's, there is no controller-in-the-loop test, and adoption obstacles are named, not tested.

Trade-offs a decision-maker would price are named (conservative vs liberal ground holding; equity among operators vs cost, with equity constraints still leaving significant savings; the dynamic bias toward long-range flights) but no curve is drawn; precursor of the price-of-fairness line (S076, card c16).

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: review as triage: best available model per class with computational performance and use to date
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Taxonomy of four classes; per section the best models, their computational record (sizes, machines, solvers) and applications, then numbered conclusions; existing name (card a3-01), confirmed in full text.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: feasibility-border test instances
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Multi-airport tests run at the critical capacities below which the problem becomes infeasible, found by trial and error, as the practically relevant and hardest regime; existing name (cards c04, s2-02); recurs in S275 (this batch, p. 25).

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: self-ranking in one's own field review, backed by a third-party comparison
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The survey ranks its authors' Bertsimas-Stock model first ('the first optimal approach', 'best performance') and leans on Andreatta-Brunetta's independent comparison, while printing the counter-evidence (about 5% savings in two of five CASA cases; feasibility unchecked).

transferable: Organize a field review per problem class: best available model, illustrative formulation, computational record with sizes and machines, applications to date, open gaps (pp. 1, 9-30).
Speed an LP with side constraints by solving the network-flow core alone for a basis, then adding the side constraints and continuing with dual simplex (p. 27).
Test integer models at the infeasibility border (tightest capacities that stay feasible), located by trial and error, and report times there (p. 30).
Use a two-flight probability-tree example to show what dynamic re-planning gains over a static plan and which systematic bias it introduces (pp. 19-22).

quotes.text: On the other hand, this evidence is very preliminary.
These models represent the strongest formulations proposed to date for this class of problems.

title: Applications of semidefinite optimization in stochastic project scheduling
contribution: Bounds expected project tardiness under first and second (joint) moment information by dualizing the moment problem into a co-positive program and restricting it to an SDP with one semidefinite constraint per path, beating the Birge-Maddox bound on its two published examples.
problem_entry: {CP + SD; AP (project scheduling)} Expected completion time is #P-complete even for independent two-valued durations, which motivates bounds (p. 1); durations are dependent and only means, variances and covariances are known in practice (p. 1); CLT approximations give no bounds and fail on small networks (pp. 1-2); Birge-Maddox bounds do not handle correlations and name it as future research (p. 2).
key_idea: Worst-case expected tardiness over all distributions with given first and second (joint) moments as a moment problem; dual by Klein Haneveld's strong duality; per-path dual constraint as co-positivity of a matrix; replaced by the sufficient condition PSD plus nonnegative, giving an SDP with |P| + 1 semidefinite constraints (pp. 2-3).
assumptions: Acyclic project network, known minimum durations a >= 0, known E[x_i] and E[x_i x_j] (pp. 1-2); tardiness upper semicontinuous so strong duality holds (pp. 2-3). Tests on Birge-Maddox's two small examples (10 activities and 3 paths; 5 activities) with a_i, E[x_i], E[x_i^2]; the cross moments used are not listed [my reading] (pp. 3-4).
proof_devices: moment-problem dual with y0 for the mass and y_i for the moments; strong duality by Klein Haneveld for upper semicontinuous tardiness (pp. 2-3)
per-path dual constraint written as a quadratic form in (w, 1) nonnegative on the orthant, i.e. co-positivity of a bordered matrix (eqs. 3-5, p. 3)
co-positivity (co-NP-complete) replaced by PSD plus entrywise nonnegative, a sufficient condition giving a valid SDP upper bound with |P| + 1 SDP constraints (eq. 6, p. 3)
higher moments via sums of squares (Parrilo) offered as an extension (p. 4)
experiments: SeDuMi; nine due dates over the two Birge-Maddox examples; the SDP bound is below Birge-Maddox in all nine (e.g. 4.16 vs 5 at T = 0 in Example 2; 0.48 vs 0.73 at T = 25 in Example 1); no solve times, no large network, no correlated instance (pp. 3-4).
positioning: Against CLT approximations (no bounds, poor for small networks) and the Birge-Maddox bound (no correlations), whose own future-research sentence is quoted; builds on Bertsimas-Popescu (pp. 1-2).
writing: Five-page note: problem, rival method outlined in detail, formulation, two tables, extensions; the abstract's 'tight upper bounds' (p. 1) against a sufficient-condition SDP in the body (p. 3) [my reading].
limits_future: Stated: SDP constraints grow with the number of paths and 'may be too huge for large networks'; remedies: critical-path screening heuristics and LP-based cutting planes for the SDP (p. 4). Extensions: higher moments by sums of squares, piecewise-quadratic tardiness, variance and overrun-probability bounds (p. 4).

method_links.note: A probability question owned by PERT analysis becomes a conic program via its dual; the boundary is printed twice: co-positivity is co-NP-complete so a tractable restriction is used (p. 3), and the path count limits scale (p. 4). Matches Method 1 steps 3-5 and the CP row of the Domain Map.

The incumbent bound is dueled on its own published examples and loses all nine comparisons, but no times are reported, there is no large instance, and the advertised advantage (correlations) is not exercised.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: assume only what can be estimated, worst-case the rest
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Only first and second (joint) moments, which practice can estimate, are assumed; the bound is distribution free; existing name (cards c08, a3-02).

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: rival's stated open problem as the entry point
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The paper quotes Birge-Maddox's own sentence that efficient solutions with limited correlation information are future research, then answers it with the SDP.

transferable: To bound a worst-case expectation of a max of linear functions under moment information, dualize, write each piece's dual constraint as co-positivity of a bordered matrix, and replace co-positivity by PSD plus entrywise nonnegative to get an SDP upper bound (pp. 2-3).
Duel a new bound on the incumbent's own published instances first, so the comparison cannot be blamed on data choice (pp. 3-4).
Name the scaling bottleneck in the conclusion with two concrete remedies (path screening; cutting planes for SDPs) (p. 4).

quotes.text: In contrast, we provide formal upper bounds that are distribution free.
The principle limitation of the current technique is that the number of semidefinite constraints it generates is proportional to the number of paths.

title: Multistage air traffic flow management under capacity uncertainty: a robust and adaptive optimization approach
contribution: Models weather-induced capacity uncertainty in network air traffic flow management by a low-dimensional weather-front set with a polyhedral convex hull, shows the robust problem is the deterministic one at row-wise worst capacities, solves the adaptive LP relaxation by (piecewise) affine policies counted by extreme points, and finds small prices of robustness on synthetic instances.
problem_entry: {RO + IO; AP} Weather caused about 60% of 2009 delays (p. 3); network ATFM models assume deterministic capacities, which 'may lead to suboptimal and possibly infeasible solutions' (p. 3); stochastic work exists only for single airports, so the paper claims the first network model under uncertainty (p. 4); stochastic programming set aside for unknown distributions and scenario growth, adaptive optimization added against RO's conservatism (pp. 4-5).
key_idea: Weather-front uncertainty set (capacity drops to alpha*C between an uncertain T_a and T_a + d, fronts propagating through phases with lags; pp. 9-13); conv(U) polyhedral and needing only the worst alpha (Theorem 1, Remark 2, p. 19); robust = deterministic TFMP at row-wise minimum capacity b_min (Theorem 2, p. 20); adaptive LP relaxation solved by affine policies on simplices and piecewise affine ones otherwise, pieces counted by extreme points (Theorem 3, Algorithm 1, pp. 21-22); b_min in U makes adaptivity worthless (Prop. 3, Corollary 1, pp. 23-24).
assumptions: Binary time-indexed TFMP with capacity, connectivity and fairness-reversal constraints (pp. 6-10); only right-hand-side capacities uncertain, A and c certain (p. 14); Assumption 1 (alpha*C integer) for practicality and to simplify the integrality proofs (p. 11); step-function capacity profiles justified on two Lincoln Labs sectors (pp. 11-12); 3-4 fronts a day (p. 12). Experiments on a synthetic 10 x 10 grid of 100 sectors with 55 major US airports and simulated fronts; the schedule source is not named in section 5 although the abstract says real-world schedules (pp. 2, 24-25).
proof_devices: Lemma 2: robust over a discrete set = robust over its convex hull (proof omitted, p. 15)
randomized rounding with one uniform threshold proves integrality of the monotone-indicator polyhedron (Prop. 1, pp. 16-17, citing the Bertsimas-Weismantel book)
convex-hull sandwich Q_alpha in Q and U in P_alpha (Prop. 2, pp. 18-19)
robust = deterministic TFMP at the row-wise minimum b_min, for any right-hand-side set (Theorem 2, p. 20)
multistage extension of Bertsimas-Goyal: affine policy as a convex combination of vertex responses on a simplex set, worst-case cost separating stage by stage (Theorem 3, pp. 21, 28-29)
extreme-point counting bounds the number of affine pieces; exponential growth printed (Tables 1-2, pp. 21-22)
b_min in U implies adaptive = robust (Prop. 3, Corollary 1, pp. 23-24)

[my reading] Lemma 1 (NP-hardness under a discrete set, proof in a 'full version') is stated for a problem with only right-hand-side uncertainty, where Theorem 2's row-wise argument would give an LP (pp. 14-15, 20)
experiments: ROME with CPLEX; times include ROME parsing, the majority of total time; no machine stated (p. 25). Robust runs (500-1,000 flights; 81 to 65,536,000 extreme points): at most 0.15% non-integral, times comparable to deterministic, price of robustness 0% to about 11.7% [my computation from Table 3] (pp. 25-26). Adaptive runs (100-150 flights; up to 4,096 extreme points): 250-813 s vs 34-133 s robust, and Z_Adapt = Z_Rob in all twelve instances, not discussed in the text (p. 26). POR grows with capacity reduction (Fig. 9, p. 27). Capacities at the infeasibility border (p. 25).
positioning: Builds on the group's own ATFM models (Bertsimas-Stock-Patterson; Bertsimas-Gupta fairness), the 1997 survey S241 and Bertsimas-Goyal on affine policies; frames stochastic programming vs robust optimization and robust vs adaptive (pp. 3-5).
writing: 'First application' and 'first attempt' claims (pp. 2, 4); lettered contributions (pp. 5-6); 'we feel' in motivating the set (p. 10); a cross-reference slip (Proposition 2 for Theorem 2, p. 20); lemma proofs deferred to a 'full version' (p. 15).
limits_future: Stated: the adaptive problem is expensive and only its LP relaxation is covered by the theory (pp. 2, 21, 25); extreme points can explode (p. 22). The outline promises 'directions for further research' (p. 6) but the conclusion gives none (pp. 27-28).

method_links.note: The robust ATFM problem is the nominal problem on modified data and keeps its integrality and solve times; the boundary of the adaptive device is printed by counting extreme points.

Prices of robustness and adaptability are defined and the robustness price is plotted against capacity reduction, but the knob is a property of the set, there is no probabilistic violation bound, and adaptivity is priced at exactly zero in every reported instance.
The 1994-2011 ATFM programme (S241, Bertsimas-Stock-Patterson, Bertsimas-Gupta) is carried into robust optimization by a new student with NSF EFRI funding.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: robust = nominal on modified data (structure inheritance)
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The robust TFMP is the deterministic TFMP at the row-wise minimum capacity, so integrality and speed carry over; existing name (card c09).

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: geometry of the uncertainty set explains the value of adaptivity
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The number of affine pieces is governed by the set's extreme points, and adaptivity gains nothing when b_min lies in the set; existing name (card s2-05).

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: own earlier result's limit as the entry
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The deterministic network models made robust are the group's own (Bertsimas-Stock-Patterson, Bertsimas-Gupta); S241 had recorded in 1997 that all multi-airport models were deterministic (S241 p. 27).

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: feasibility-border test instances
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Capacities set at the 'infeasibility border', values that turn infeasible when perturbed conservatively; also S241 (p. 30).

transferable: Build the uncertainty set from a low-dimensional physical driver (a weather front's arrival time, duration and depth, propagated through phases) so its extreme points can be counted and the policy complexity bounded (pp. 9-13, 21-22).
Prove integrality of a monotone-indicator polyhedron by randomized rounding with one uniform threshold: the rounded solution is feasible and its expected cost equals the LP value (pp. 16-17).
With right-hand-side-only uncertainty, check first whether the robust problem is just the nominal problem at the row-wise worst case before building any reformulation (p. 20).
Before solving an adaptive model, test whether the worst-case vector lies in the set; if so adaptivity cannot help (Prop. 3, pp. 23-24).

quotes.text: Assumption 1. We assume that the value of α is such that αC is an integer because of two reasons: i) it is not practical to have fractional capacity and ii) the integrality proofs presented later become simplified as a result of this assumption.

The key insight from the plot is that when bmin is “close” to the deterministic capacity, the price of robustness is quite small and the deterministic schedule can be adjusted to make it feasible for uncertain scenarios.

title: Channel Coding via Robust Optimization Part 2: The Multi-User Channel
contribution: Extends the robust-optimization approach to finite-length channel coding to two-user interference, multi-access and multicast channels: a rank-minimization SDP (Gaussian noise) or mixed binary LP (exponential noise) whose solution gives an achievable rate with a code or non-achievability on a slightly noisier channel, computed for n = 60 with approximate upper bounds.
problem_entry: {RO + CP + IO; AP (information theory)} Capacity regions of interference and multicast channels are open and random coding does not characterize them (pp. 1-2); finite-length results exist for multi-access but not interference channels (pp. 2-3); problem: decide whether a rate pair is achievable for given n, powers, gains, sigma and epsilon, and construct the code (pp. 3-4).
key_idea: Part 1's moves for two users: typical sets as uncertainty sets, binaries that count probabilities, reformulation as mixed binary LP or nonconvex QP (p. 2); a counting decoder that is maximum likelihood for noise uniform in a ball (Prop. 1, pp. 4-5); rank minimization under SDP constraints (eq. 33, p. 9): rank 1 means achievable with codebooks, rank >= 2 means not achievable at noise (1 + 3 nu) sigma (Algorithm 3, Theorem 1, p. 10); multi-access and multicast as special cases (p. 18); exponential noise as a mixed binary LP (Algorithm 8, Theorem 4, pp. 24-25).
assumptions: Two-user Gaussian interference channel with powers P1, P2, real gains h12, h21 and average error epsilon (pp. 3-4); noise replaced by T deterministic sphere vectors as in Part 1, with a 'cushion' delta1 so guarantees cover all Gaussian noise (pp. 5-6); accuracy knob nu (p. 5). No data; instances P1 = 1.5, P2 = 2, h = 0.3 and P1 = 10, P2 = 20, h12 = 0.2, h21 = 0.25 (pp. 25, 27).
proof_devices: counting decoder = maximum likelihood decoder for noise uniform in a ball (Prop. 1, pp. 4-5)
counting binaries with decoding constraints and a cushion delta1 so finitely many noise samples certify all Gaussian noise (pp. 5-9)
rank-1 lifting Y = y y' of the nonconvex feasibility problem into rank minimization with SDP constraints (eq. 33, p. 9)
two-sided rate test: rank 1 achievable, rank >= 2 not achievable on the noisier channel (Theorem 1, p. 10)

averaging proposition, Gaussian-to-uniform noise transfer, Wyner's sphere covering and Gaussian concentration (Props. 2-6, pp. 11-12); part (b) by contrapositive (pp. 12-13); uniform noise used inside the proof for its simpler decoder (p. 16)
Fazel et al.'s log-det heuristic for rank minimization (p. 25)
experiments: Gaussian interference channel only, n = 60, epsilon = 0.001, nu = 0.05; about 1 billion variables split into 5,000 SDPARA instances of about 200,000 variables; 40 h on an 8-processor, 48 GB Linux machine (p. 25). RO lower bounds said to dominate Carleial's and Han-Kobayashi's asymptotic lower bounds and RO upper bounds Etkin et al.'s asymptotic upper bounds (Figs. 1-2, pp. 25-27). No multi-access, multicast or exponential computations. [my reading] Finite-length bounds are set against asymptotic ones with the uncertified upper bound; coupling across the 5,000 subproblems is not explained (pp. 11, 25).
positioning: Network information theory (Ahlswede, Liao, Han-Kobayashi, Etkin et al., Carleial); finite-length results only for multi-access channels (Huang-Moulin, MolavianJazi-Laneman); extends Part 1 (Bandi-Bertsimas 2015) (pp. 1-3).
writing: The abstract states the uncertified upper bound plainly (p. 1); the discussion after Theorem 1 separates 'in principle' from numerics (pp. 10-11); dominance claims in section 5 are stated without numbers (pp. 25-26).
limits_future: Stated in abstract and body: no provable optimality, so the lower bound is valid with a code and the upper bound is only an approximation (pp. 1, 3, 11). The conclusion restates results, with no limits or future work (p. 27). Not read: most of the proof (pp. 13-18), multi-access and multicast derivations (pp. 19-24), Appendices (pp. 29-35).

method_links.note: A problem owned by information theory is written as an optimization problem whose class follows the noise model (rank-constrained SDP for Gaussian, mixed binary LP for exponential and uniform noise).

Certificate status labelled honestly (valid lower bound with a code, approximate upper bound), but no warm start, no stated stopping rule (Part 1 printed 50,000 restarts, card s2-06), and the duel is with asymptotic bounds, not a finite-length incumbent.
Part 2 of the robust-probability programme with Bandi, by then Kellogg faculty; still listed as submitted on the homepage (card a3-03).

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: asymmetric certificate labelling
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Constructed codes certify the lower bounds; the upper bounds are called approximations in the abstract, contributions and discussion; existing name (card s2-06, S554).

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: limit laws as primitives
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Shannon's typical sets serve as uncertainty sets for the two-user channels; existing name (cards s09, s2-06).

transferable: Replace a hard decoder by the maximum-likelihood decoder of a simpler noise (uniform in a ball), prove by a transfer proposition that it suffices for the target noise, and build the optimization around the simple decoder (pp. 4-5, 11-12, 16).

Get a two-sided rate test from one optimization (feasible means achievable on a slightly cleaner channel, infeasible means not achievable on a slightly noisier one), with the gap governed by one knob nu (p. 10).
Add a cushion to constraints written on a finite sample of noise vectors so the guarantees extend to the whole distribution (pp. 5-6).

quotes.text: In this way, the upper bound we report can only be seen as an approximation.
The resulting semidefinite optimization problems for n = 60 involved around 1 billion variables.

title: A scalable algorithm for sparse and robust portfolios
contribution: Solves cardinality-constrained, ridge-regularized Markowitz problems to provable optimality by an outer-approximation method driven by closed-form dual subgradients, with a discrete ADMM warm start, embedded local search and an SOCP lower bound, beating CPLEX and Gurobi big-M formulations by orders of magnitude on OR-library sets and reaching index scale (arXiv v1 of S136).
problem_entry: {IO + CP + RO; AP (finance); ML via the regression link} Cardinality-constrained Markowitz with minimum investments and linear constraints (pp. 1-2); Table 1 dates the frontier: no exact method reliably beyond 300 securities while real problems choose from 500-5,000 (p. 3); the finance community treats the problem as intractable and uses heuristics or l1 surrogates (p. 3); the l1 surrogate fails under nonnegativity and buys robustness, not sparsity (Theorem 1, pp. 3-4).
key_idea: Dualize the continuous inner problem (Theorem 3, pp. 8-9) into a saddle point convex in the support (Theorem 4, p. 10); closed-form objective and subgradients (Corollaries 1-2, p. 11) drive Kelley's outer approximation in one branch-and-cut tree with lazy callbacks and feasibility cuts (pp. 11-12); accelerators: ADMM warm start from 5 random starts with L = 10 (pp. 13-14), local search when a cut is within 5% of the incumbent (p. 14), SOCP lower bound added after 100 cuts (Theorem 6, Algorithm 3, pp. 14-17).
assumptions: Long-only, fully invested, ||x||_0 <= k, ridge 1/(2 gamma)||x||^2, risk weight sigma on the variance (the experiments use the equivalent form with a weight alpha on the return term) (pp. 1-2, 18); Assumption 1, a constraint qualification (pp. 8-9); sparsity motivated by transaction and monitoring costs and fees for index tracking (p. 7). Data: OR-library port1-port5 (31-225 assets); Yahoo! Finance daily closes 2007-2017 for S&P 500, Russell 1000, Wilshire 5000, SVD low-rank covariances, days with over 20% price change omitted (pp. 18, 20-21).
proof_devices: Theorem 1: l1-penalized portfolio = robust to box errors in expected returns (cited from Ben-Tal et al., p. 4)
Theorem 2: Markowitz = worst-case return over an ellipsoid (Lagrangian duality and KKT, cited, p. 6)
portfolio-regression equivalence via Sigma = X'X (pp. 7-8)
inner dual under a constraint qualification and a saddle point by Sion-Kakutani (Theorems 3-4, pp. 8-10)
closed-form objective and subgradients from the inner dual (Corollaries 1-2, p. 11)
Kelley outer approximation with feasibility cuts in one tree via lazy callbacks; finite convergence by Fletcher-Leyffer, exponential worst case admitted (pp. 11-12)

SOCP lower bound via minimax and LP duality over the capped simplex (Theorem 6, pp. 14-15); exactness as a sufficient condition for support recovery, 'not universally satisfiable' (Corollary 3, pp. 15-16)
experiments: Julia/JuMP 0.18.0, CPLEX 12.8.0, Gurobi 7.5.1 on a Xeon E5-2600 v4 cluster; Algorithm 3 single-threaded, big-M solvers on 28 threads (p. 17). OR-library: 0.59-91.27 s vs up to the 36,000 s limit for CPLEX and Gurobi big-M (Table 2, p. 19). S&P 500 about 105-374 s, Russell 1000 about 1,730-4,770 s; gap not closed in 36,000 s for gamma = 100/sqrt(n) (up to 1.157%); Wilshire 5000 from 8 s to the 36,000 s limit (Tables 3-5, pp. 21-22); SOCP bound plus 500 s gives 1-2% (p. 23). Hyperparameter sensitivity (pp. 24-26). No out-of-sample portfolio test [my reading].
positioning: A table of each rival method's largest solved instance (Shioda, Frangioni-Gentile, Vielma et al., Bonami-Lejeune, Gao-Li, Cui et al.) (pp. 2-3); l1 surrogates (DeMiguel, Brodie) reinterpreted as robustness (pp. 3-4); generalizes Bertsimas-Van Parys (pp. 4, 8); related to lift-and-project and perspective cuts but without variable explosion (p. 27).
writing: Three experimental questions answered in a numbered summary (pp. 18, 26); headline numbers (3-4 orders of magnitude, 5,000 securities) scoped in the body (pp. 1, 21-23, 26); interpretive asides: a Bayesian reading of gamma, a ranked-list policy, competitors' private information (pp. 6, 24-25).
limits_future: Exponential worst case (p. 12); single thread because JuMP is not thread-safe (p. 17); gaps open at large gamma (p. 21). Future: chance and buy-in constraints through conic duality (p. 27). Versions [card s15, S136]: the IJOC version drops 'robust' from the title, moves the frontier to 400 securities, adds MISOCO and Frangioni-Gentile opponents with printed failures, runs on a laptop with code on GitHub, and keeps robustness only by citation.

method_links.note: Heuristic warm start, exact solve with stated time limit, tolerance, solver versions and machine, certificates or printed gaps, and a duel with the commercial solvers' standard big-M formulation; the thread difference (28 vs 1) is disclosed and favours the incumbents (p. 17); Gurobi's tolerance is looser (p. 19).

Structure read off the dual (subgradients, primal recovery), a conic SOCP relaxation, and the boundary printed (exponential worst case; unclosed gaps at large gamma). Also full-text evidence for Heuristic 1: the l1 surrogate buys robustness, not sparsity (p. 4).
The intractability belief is named and dated by a table of each method's largest solved instance, then reopened by an algorithm, without a solver x hardware figure.
Robustness knobs (gamma, alpha) are interpreted and their effect on the chosen support mapped (stable supports, ranked-list reading), but no price curve or out-of-sample property is measured.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: exact dictionary between a statistical procedure and a robust model, with its boundary
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: l1 surrogate = robustness to return errors (Theorem 1) and Markowitz = worst-case return (Theorem 2), with the boundary that the surrogate cannot be used under nonnegativity and rarely solves the sparse problem; full-text evidence for Heuristic 1; existing name (card c19).

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: exact equivalence to a sibling problem the group already solves
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Portfolio selection rewritten as constrained sparse regression via Sigma = X'X, importing Bertsimas-Van Parys's cutting-plane machinery; existing name (card s15).

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: level the field and say which way it still tilts
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The big-M solvers get 28 threads and Algorithm 3 one, with the reason (JuMP not thread-safe) stated; tolerances differ (Gurobi 1e-8 vs 1e-12).

transferable: Turn a cardinality-constrained convex QP into a saddle point convex in the support by dualizing the inner problem; the inner dual gives objective values and subgradients in closed form for Kelley cuts (pp. 9-11).
Run local search inside the branch-and-cut tree only when a new cut's objective is within 5% of the incumbent, and inject improvements by heuristic callback (p. 14).
Delay an uninformative global lower bound (the SOCP) until a heuristic has found a near-optimal solution (after 100 cuts) so it does not distort early branching (p. 16).
Print a table of the largest instance each rival method reliably solved, to define 'at scale' before the experiments (p. 3).

quotes.text: Due to both the difficulties encountered during the above attempts at solving the Markowitz model at scale, and Problem (1)’s NP-hardness, the greater finance community considers Problem (1) to be intractable and uses two approaches as surrogates.
Moreover, the parameter ρ promotes robustness, rather than sparsity.

title: New Methods of Natural Language Processing using Machine Learning Methods to Identify Ischemic Stroke Presence, Acuity and Location from Clinical Radiology Reports
contribution: A one-page clinical abstract (MLHC 2018) comparing text featurizations and interpretable and opaque classifiers for detecting ischemic stroke in 1,357 radiology reports, reporting AUC 0.951 (BOW with logistic regression) against 0.976 (GloVe with deep learning) and judging the cost of interpretability low; precursor of S144.
problem_entry: {ML + AP; DA} Radiology text holds patient-specific information that studies either ignore or hand-label at small scale; ICD-9/10 codes misclassify ischemic stroke and give neither acuity nor location; earlier classifiers stopped short of acuity and location (p. 1).
key_idea: BOW and TF-IDF features plus GloVe embeddings trained on a compiled neurology corpus, crossed with interpretable and opaque classifiers (logistic regression, k-NN, OCT, random forest, RNN); stroke presence reported as preliminary (p. 1).
assumptions: 1,357 head CT/CTA and brain MRI/MRA reports of adults with ischemic-stroke codes, 2003-2018, MGH and Brigham registry, hand-labelled by two clinicians; 925 (68%) report stroke (p. 1). Split, validation protocol and labeller agreement not given [my reading] (p. 1).
experiments: BOW + logistic regression AUC 0.951; GloVe + deep learning AUC 0.976; called a 2.1% improvement, which by my arithmetic is 2.5 AUC points (2.6% relative); OCT's result not reported; the conclusion's 'high sensitivity and specificity' has no numbers behind it (p. 1).
positioning: Earlier ML text classification (pneumonia, breast cancer, stroke, head CT critical findings) did not reach acuity and location (p. 1).
writing: Structured clinical abstract (Background, Methods, Results, Conclusion); the conclusion asserts sensitivity and specificity the results do not report (p. 1).
limits_future: Acuity, size and severity left for further study; embeddings to be released (p. 1). Versions [card c22, S144]: the 2020 paper reports 1,359 reports and external validation, where BOW with logistic regression did not generalize as well as GloVe with an RNN (S144 p. 9), so the low price of interpretability held only internally.

method_links.note: The price of interpretability is stated as one number and judged 'not high', but it is a single point with no knob, curve or bound, and the number does not follow from the two AUCs [my computation]; the abstract card a3-03 had called it evidence.
The owner's current rule (billing codes) motivates the work but is not scored as a baseline; AUC, not a decision metric.
Health-programme cohort step: ORC students and alumni (Zhang, Orfanoudaki, Caprasse) with a clinician first author in a clinical track.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: interpretable-versus-complex pair carried to external validation
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Internal-only stage of the S144 pattern: BOW + logistic regression vs GloVe + deep learning priced at 2.1% and the interpretable pair judged adequate, before the external cohort of S144 reversed the reading (card c22); existing name.

transferable: Train word embeddings on a compiled domain corpus (online encyclopedias, neurology textbooks, disease papers, radiology reports) and release them with the study (p. 1).
State the interpretable-versus-opaque comparison as one priced difference per task (here AUC 0.951 vs 0.976) so clinical readers see what interpretability costs (p. 1).
coauthors: Charlene Jennifer Ong (first), Rebecca Zhang, Agni Orfanoudaki, Francois Pierre M. Caprasse, Meghan Hutch, Liang Ma, Darian Fard, Margaret Minnig, Stelios Smirnakis; Bertsimas last

quotes.text: The cost of interpretability is not high in this setting, as the latter is associated with only a 2.1% improvement.

The high sensitivity and specificity of our models in identifying stroke is consistent with other work in the literature and is a model for an improved approach of identifying stroke from large data cohorts for both clinical and research use.

title: Early Detection of Opioid Over-Procurement: A Machine Learning Approach
contribution: Detects opioid over-procurement by pharmacies from DEA ARCOS data with unsupervised (DTW clustering), supervised (DTW k-NN plus OCT) and semi-supervised (matrix completion) models trained on forensic Walgreens labels, reaching out-of-sample AUC above 0.97 and estimating up to 600 million pills preventable (the 2020 version of S622).
problem_entry: {ML + AP; DA} The prescription-opioid crisis and its costs (pp. 1-2); prior ML predicts patient risk or online sellers, so the paper claims the first models flagging supply-chain entities (p. 2); the timing argument is a 2020 GAO recommendation that the DEA use algorithms on ARCOS data (p. 2).
key_idea: Three detectors indexed by label availability (p. 6): DTW distances with complete-linkage clustering, small clusters suspicious (pp. 6-7); DTW k-NN plus OCT on the reporter-buyer adjacency matrix, averaged (pp. 7-8); matrix completion with side information and a rank-k discrete formulation solved by OptComplete, monthly probabilities combined per zip code (pp. 8-10); the semi-supervised setting 'most closely resembles the true nature of the data' (p. 6).
assumptions: DEA ARCOS: about 380 million transactions, 76.5 billion pills, 2006-2012; oxycodone plus hydrocodone by buyer and month (p. 3). Labels: 308 Walgreens buyers flagged from a DOJ settlement, court records, the Washington Post and a distributor report (pp. 4, 19-20); 206 of 5,441 zip codes flagged (3.8%); mail-order buyers excluded (pp. 5-6). Admitted: state over-representation in labels (p. 5); labels taken as ground truth, 'a necessary assumption' (p. 8). 80/20 stratified split (p. 6).
proof_devices: DTW distance (fast DTW) with complete-linkage agglomerative clustering and the elbow rule (pp. 6-7)
matrix completion with side information through a sparsity-selected factor of rank k (eq. 3) solved by OptComplete, entries clipped to [0, 1] afterwards, hyperparameters by grid search (p. 9)
zip-code violation probability from monthly entries, or the conservative maximum (pp. 9-10)
experiments: Out-of-sample AUC by training year (Table 2, p. 10): matrix completion 0.937-0.983, combined supervised 0.909-0.994, OCT 0.840-0.959, k-NN 0.747-0.931, clustering about 0.70. Inter-model agreement at 3.8% and 10% positive rates, matrix completion vs supervised above 80% (p. 12). Impact: above-median pills to flagged zip codes after the intervention year, up to 600 million (5% of Walgreens' pills) with a system in place by end-2006 (p. 13); CVS transfer flags 62 zip codes, up to 160 million pills (p. 14). No baseline from the DEA's current rules. [my reading] Labels come from records dated 2013-2020 (pp. 15, 17) and the split is random over zip codes (p. 6), so 'early detection' varies the input window, not when labels would have been known.
positioning: Demand-side patient-risk models and Twitter-based seller detection cited as different problems; 'first paper' claim; timeliness from the GAO report (p. 2).
writing: Short applied paper; impact stated in pills by intervention year; a DEA-facing conclusion (p. 14); the flagged-buyer list printed in full in the appendix (pp. 19-20).
limits_future: Stated: label over-representation (p. 5), labels as ground truth (p. 8), agreement as a proxy for accuracy (p. 12). Future: the DEA's Suspicious Orders Report System (October 2019) as more authoritative labels (p. 12). Versions [card a3-04, S622 abstract]: the published version reports AUC 0.87 and compares against three established DEA rules, finding high false-positive and false-negative rates.

method_links.note: The owner (the DEA) and a decision-level outcome (pills an intervention would have stopped) are named, but the owner's current rules are not scored, the counterfactual counts every above-median pill as preventable, and nothing is field-tested; the published version adds the DEA rules as baseline (card a3-04), as Method 5 step 2 asks.

The group's OCT is one ensemble component with no time limit, warm start or gap reported, compared with k-NN rather than CART; the paper writes 'optimal' in quotation marks (p. 8). Context: Tension T1.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: counterfactual replay against the historical decision-maker
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Variant: the replay is against no intervention (pills distributed to flagged zip codes after each possible intervention year), not against the regulator's rules; existing name.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: forensic labels from legal and press records, checked by inter-model agreement
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Ground truth assembled from a DOJ settlement, court records, newspaper and distributor reports, listed buyer by buyer, then validated by agreement between independent models at the label prevalence.

transferable: When ground truth is scarce, build a suite indexed by label availability (unsupervised, semi-supervised, supervised) and report all three so readers can choose by how many labels they hold (pp. 6-10).
Without authoritative labels, report pairwise agreement between independent models at a positive rate fixed to the label prevalence, and again at a looser rate (p. 12).
State impact in decision units (pills by intervention year) at a threshold calibrated to the label prevalence, and test transfer to a second operator with the same threshold (pp. 12-14).

quotes.text: Note that when training these models, we treat the labels as ground-truth, which is a necessary assumption given the data available.
The rationale behind this approach is that in the absence of authoritative labels, consistency between models is an indicator of predictive accuracy.
